summary.text: At \(n=1\), the sum has only the \(k=0\) term, with \(\beta(0)=t(0)=1\), so \(a(1)=8/2=4\), which is even. But \(1=2^0\) is a power of two, directly contradicting the claimed parity equivalence.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\beta(k)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}^{2}\binom{k+j}{j},
\]
and let \(t(k)\) be the coefficient of \(x^k\) in
\[
(x^2+4x-1)^k.
\]
The sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^k(15k+8)\beta(k)t(k)
\qquad(n>0).
\]
We disprove the claimed parity characterization by taking \(n=1\).

First compute the two auxiliary quantities that occur in the sole summand. For \(k=0\), the sum defining \(\beta(0)\) has only \(j=0\), so
\[
\beta(0)=\binom00^2\binom00=1^2\cdot 1=1.
\]
Also,
\[
(x^2+4x-1)^0=1,
\]
whose coefficient of \(x^0\) is \(1\). Hence
\[
t(0)=1.
\]

When \(n=1\), the outer sum defining \(a(n)\) runs from \(k=0\) to \(k=n-1=0\), and therefore contains exactly one term. Substituting the values just found gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(1)
&=\frac1{2\cdot1}(-1)^0(15\cdot0+8)\beta(0)t(0)\\
&=\frac12\cdot1\cdot8\cdot1\cdot1\\
&=4.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(a(1)\) is indeed an integer, but it is even, since \(4=2\cdot2\); in particular, \(a(1)\) is not odd.

On the other hand, \(1\) is a positive power of two in the usual sense used in the conjecture: a natural number is a power of two if it equals \(2^r\) for some nonnegative integer \(r\), and
\[
1=2^0.
\]
Moreover, \(n=1\) satisfies the required condition \(n>0\).

Consequently, at the positive index \(n=1\), the statement “\(n\) is a power of two” is true while the statement “\(a(n)\) is odd” is false. Hence the asserted equivalence
\[
a(n)\text{ is odd}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\text{ is a power of two}
\]
fails. Since the conjecture claims this equivalence, together with integrality, for every \(n>0\), this single counterexample disproves the entire conjunction, regardless of the fact that \(a(1)=4\) is itself integral.
